$comment: Lanternlight Claude Code settings. Windows paths MUST use forward slashes - a single backslash makes this file invalid JSON, and an unparseable settings file registers no hooks and warns about nothing. The PreToolUse matcher MUST name every shell tool that can reach git: this machine is PowerShell-primary, and a matcher of 'Bash' alone let a commit issued through the PowerShell tool bypass the gate entirely. Measured 2026-08-09. Attribution is BLANKED, not merely unset: CLAUDE.md forbids a Co-Authored-By trailer as operator policy, and the harness injects one by default. Both the current key (attribution.commit) and the deprecated one (includeCoAuthoredBy) are set, because an older client reads only the latter and would reintroduce the trailer silently. Set 2026-09-06. The SessionStart hook runs ops/inbox_watch.py for ROADMAP OPS-33, and it deliberately differs from the other two in two ways: it uses python.exe rather than pythonw.exe, because the session must SEE its stdout and pythonw suppresses the console, and it carries NO matcher, because an omitted matcher runs on every start while a matcher regex that fails to match is a hook that silently never fires. Added 2026-09-06 with operator approval. The second PostToolUse entry runs tools/syntax_check_hook.py for ROADMAP OPS-37: it compiles each edited .py and reports an unparseable file on stderr at the moment it is written, because a hook interpreter here is windowless and a broken file is otherwise silent until a much later test run. It carries an EXPLICIT matcher rather than none - an omitted matcher fires on every tool, including Read and Bash, where there is nothing to compile - and it names NotebookEdit alongside Edit and Write because the hook also reads notebook_path. It exits 0 on every path by design; a PostToolUse hook that exits non-zero breaks the session it runs in. It uses python.exe rather than the pythonw.exe of the two hooks above, so its report is not routed through an interpreter chosen for having no console; the accepted cost is the same one the SessionStart hook already pays. Added 2026-09-07. The UserPromptSubmit hook runs ops/inbox_watch.py --on-prompt for ROADMAP OPS-41: it acknowledges the inbox ONCE per session on the operator's own turn, which is the event SessionStart cannot be - SessionStart fires for subagents too and a hook on it cannot tell them apart. It carries NO matcher, because UserPromptSubmit takes none and a matcher regex that fails to match is a hook that silently never fires. It uses pythonw.exe and prints nothing on every path, because a UserPromptSubmit hook's stdout is injected into the session context; and it exits 0 on every path, because exit code 2 on this event BLOCKS the operator's prompt. Added 2026-09-07. The Stop hook runs ops/stop_audit.py --stop-hook for ROADMAP OPS-45: it reads the transcript the harness names in the payload, checks the final main-agent turn's numeric suite claims and file-creation claims against ground truth, and writes a report and a trace under ops/runtime/stop_audit/. It carries NO matcher, because Stop takes none. It uses pythonw.exe and prints nothing, and it exits 0 on EVERY path by design - exit code 2 on this event refuses to let the session stop and feeds stderr back to the model, which is a loop rather than a warning. It runs a pytest collection only when the turn actually asserted a number. Added 2026-09-08. EVERY HOOK COMMAND REACHES ITS SCRIPT THROUGH $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, never through an absolute repository root - ROADMAP OPS-61, changed 2026-09-08. Until then all six named C:/Lanternlight, and each hook script resolves its repo root from its own __file__, so in a clone at another path and in every git worktree - which is where lane sessions run - the hook FIRED, SUCCEEDED, and answered about a different repository without saying so. That is worse than not firing: a hook that does not fire reports nothing. Measured end-to-end before the change, in a real clone at a foreign path and in a real git worktree: the harness expands $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR itself, so it does not depend on the shell, and it resolved to the running tree for all five events this file registers - SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse and Stop. The script path is QUOTED because a clone can live under a path containing a space: at such a path the quoted form ran the clone's own script with the space intact in argv[0] and the unquoted form produced no witness at all. The quoting is why this file now carries JSON-escaped quotes, which is the reason tests/test_no_hardcoded_home_path.py narrowed its blanket no-backslash assertion to no-Windows-path-separator - a backslash before a JSON escape character cannot break the parse, and the parse is asserted separately. tools/hook_command_guard.py now fails on any hook command naming an absolute path, generalised past this one string for the reason OPS-38 had to generalise twice. OPS-70, 2026-09-10: the three path entries in permissions.allow still read Read(//C/Lanternlight/**), Write(//C/Lanternlight/**) and Edit(//C/Lanternlight/**), and that is a DECISION rather than an oversight. Whether the permission matcher expands $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR was the open question, and it does not. A Read or Edit rule's content is gitignore syntax with exactly four anchors - //path from the filesystem root, ~/path from the home directory, /path from the settings source, and a bare or ./-led path from the working directory - and no environment variable is substituted into any of them, so the OPS-61 fix does not carry across. On the same two non-observational sources named in the next sentence, the matcher normalises a path to POSIX form on Windows before matching, which is why the absolute spelling of this drive appears as //C/... rather than C:/..., and //C/Lanternlight/** is therefore believed to be the correct absolute form rather than a typo. That sentence used to be stated flat here, as though somebody had watched the normalisation happen, and an OPS-70 refutation pass on 2026-09-10 objected that nobody had: it is read off documentation and off client source, and it is written as an inference so that a later reader does not inherit it as a measurement. Two sources agree and NEITHER IS AN OBSERVATION OF A MATCH ON THIS MACHINE: the published permissions documentation, and the shipped client's own rule-anchoring code read on this machine. What could not be measured is named rather than glossed. The session that wrote this ran in bypass permissions mode, where every tool call is pre-approved regardless of the allow list, so a did-it-prompt test here cannot tell a MATCHED rule from a BYPASSED one and would have returned a false green. Settling it needs a session in default permission mode, in a clone at a different path, observing whether an Edit inside that clone is pre-approved. The consequence of keeping these three, stated so nobody reads them as portable: on the same two non-observational sources they are expected to match in this checkout and nowhere else, so a clone or a git worktree would prompt for the writes this file pre-approves here. Read that as the predicted consequence of the anchoring rule above rather than as a behaviour anyone watched, because it was not observed either - bypass permissions mode hides a MATCHED rule behind a BYPASSED one in THIS checkout exactly as thoroughly as it would in a clone, so the session that wrote this had no more evidence for the half of the sentence about here than for the half about elsewhere. That is a nuisance rather than a wrong answer, which is why they are kept rather than deleted - deleting them would also remove a pre-approval that is correct here, and no measurement says it should go. The documented portable successor is a rule anchored at the settings source, Edit(/**) rather than Edit(//C/Lanternlight/**), and it is deliberately NOT adopted here: it is a live change to what this machine pre-approves, and it is exactly the class of claim this session could not observe. tools/hook_command_guard.py now reads permissions.allow, permissions.deny, permissions.ask and permissions.additionalDirectories as well as hooks.*, and pins these three rules by their exact strings, so a fourth absolute permission rule turns the suite red.
